q: Your setInterval callback always reads the initial state value even after it changes. What is happening?
options: setInterval runs in a separate thread
The callback closed over the initial value and never updates
State updates are async so they arrive too late
setInterval blocks the event loop
explain: The callback forms a closure over the value at creation time. When state updates the closure still holds the old reference. Use a ref or functional update pattern to always read the latest value.

q: You have a Promise chain where one .then() throws. Which .catch() handles it?
options: The .catch() before the throwing .then()
The next .catch() after the throwing .then()
All .catch() handlers in the chain
None — thrown errors in .then() are unhandled
explain: Errors propagate down the chain and are caught by the next .catch() after the point of failure. A .catch() before it never sees the error.

q: You run Promise.all() with 5 promises and the third one rejects. What happens to the other 4?
options: They are all cancelled immediately
They continue running but their results are ignored
They are paused until you handle the rejection
The first two results are returned the rest cancelled
explain: Promises are not cancellable in native JS. Promise.all() rejects immediately on the first failure but the other promises keep running — you just never get their results.

q: Which queue runs first after the call stack empties — microtask or macrotask?
options: Macrotask queue — it has higher priority
Microtask queue — it fully drains before any macrotask runs
They alternate — one microtask then one macrotask
Whichever was queued first
explain: After the call stack empties the microtask queue drains completely before any macrotask runs. Promise callbacks are microtasks. setTimeout callbacks are macrotasks.

q: You store an object in a WeakMap. The object goes out of scope everywhere else. What happens?
options: The WeakMap throws an error
The WeakMap entry is garbage collected automatically
The object stays alive because WeakMap holds a reference
WeakMap converts it to a regular key
explain: WeakMap holds weak references. If no other reference to the key object exists it becomes eligible for garbage collection and the WeakMap entry disappears.

q: Your generator function yields 3 values. You call .next() a 4th time. What do you get?
options: It throws a StopIteration error
It returns the first value again
It returns { value: undefined, done: true }
It returns null
explain: Once a generator is exhausted every subsequent .next() call returns { value: undefined, done: true }. There is no error.

q: You use Object.defineProperty to make a property non-writable. Someone tries to change it in strict mode. What happens?
options: The change silently fails
It throws a TypeError
The property is deleted instead
It creates a new property with the same name
explain: In strict mode writing to a non-writable property throws a TypeError. In non-strict mode it silently fails.

q: You use a Proxy to intercept property reads on an object. What trap do you define?
options: set trap
intercept trap
get trap
access trap
explain: The get trap intercepts property reads. The set trap intercepts property writes. has intercepts the in operator. deleteProperty intercepts delete.

q: You need to make an object iterable with a for...of loop. What must you implement?
options: A .forEach() method
The Symbol.iterator method returning an iterator
A .next() method directly on the object
Extend the Array class
explain: An object is iterable if it has a Symbol.iterator method that returns an iterator object with a .next() method. for...of calls Symbol.iterator automatically.

q: You call an async function without await and it throws. Where does the error go?
options: It crashes the application
It is logged to console automatically
It becomes an unhandled Promise rejection
It is silently ignored
explain: Without await or .catch() the rejected Promise has no handler. This becomes an unhandledRejection event. In Node.js recent versions this crashes the process.

q: You add properties to objects inside a loop in different orders each time. V8 slows down. Why?
options: V8 has a property limit per object
Inconsistent property order breaks V8's hidden class optimization
Loop-created objects are stored differently in memory
V8 only optimizes objects with fewer than 10 properties
explain: V8 creates hidden classes for objects with the same shape. Adding properties in different orders creates different hidden classes breaking inline cache optimization.

q: You use structuredClone() to deep clone an object with a function property. What happens?
options: The function is cloned perfectly
The function is converted to a string
structuredClone throws a DataCloneError
The function property is set to null
explain: structuredClone does not support functions, Symbols, or DOM nodes. It throws a DataCloneError if it encounters them.

q: Memory usage grows every time a user opens a modal with event listeners. What is likely wrong?
options: Modals are too large for the DOM
Event listeners are added on open but never removed on close
The modal component is not using const
addEventListener has a memory leak by design
explain: Event listeners hold references to their callbacks. If you never call removeEventListener the listener and everything it references stays in memory even after the modal closes.

q: You call Promise.race() with 3 promises. The first resolves then the second rejects. What is the final result?
options: The rejection overrides the resolution
Both results are returned as an array
The resolved value — first settled wins permanently
It depends on timing
explain: Promise.race() resolves or rejects with the first settled promise. Once settled the result is final. Subsequent resolutions or rejections are completely ignored.

q: You use Symbol as an object key. Can JSON.stringify serialize it?
options: Yes Symbols are serialized as strings
No Symbol keys are silently omitted
Only if you use Symbol.for()
It throws a TypeError
explain: JSON.stringify silently drops Symbol-keyed properties along with functions and undefined values.

q: You use tagged template literals. What does the tag function receive as its first argument?
options: The full template string as one string
An array of the static string parts
An array of the interpolated values
The template string split by spaces
explain: The tag function receives an array of static string segments as the first argument and the interpolated values as remaining arguments.

q: You need to flatten a deeply nested array of unknown depth. What is the cleanest one-liner?
options: array.flat()
array.reduce((a, b) => a.concat(b))
array.flat(Infinity)
JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(array)).flat()
explain: flat() with no argument only flattens one level. Passing Infinity recursively flattens all levels regardless of depth.

q: You use for...in on an array and get unexpected keys. Why?
options: for...in only works on objects not arrays
for...in iterates enumerable properties including inherited ones
Arrays need for...of to access indices
for...in skips numeric keys by design
explain: for...in iterates all enumerable properties including prototype chain properties. If anything has been added to Array.prototype you will see those too.

q: You implement memoization but memory usage keeps growing. What is missing?
options: A cache size limit or expiry strategy
Memoization only works with pure functions
You need to use WeakMap instead of Map
The function is not returning the cached value correctly
explain: A naive memoization cache grows forever. In production you need an eviction strategy — max size with LRU eviction, TTL expiry, or WeakMap for automatic garbage collection.

q: You write a curried function. add(2)(3) works but add(2, 3) does not. How do you support both?
options: You cannot — currying and regular calls are mutually exclusive
Use default parameters to handle the second argument
Check arguments.length and return a function or result accordingly
Use the rest operator to collect all arguments
explain: Auto-currying checks if enough arguments were provided. If yes execute immediately. If not return a function waiting for the rest.

q: You use async/await inside a forEach loop but the awaits don't pause execution. Why?
options: forEach does not support async callbacks
forEach ignores the returned Promise from async callbacks
await only works in the outermost async function
You need to use await forEach() instead
explain: forEach calls your callback and ignores whatever it returns including Promises. Use for...of with await or Promise.all with map instead.

q: You use Proxy to validate object writes. A deeply nested property is set directly. Does your trap fire?
options: Yes Proxy intercepts all nested writes automatically
No the set trap only fires for direct property writes on the proxied object
Only if you set deep: true in the Proxy options
Only for the first level of nesting
explain: A Proxy only intercepts operations on the object it directly wraps. Nested objects are plain objects. To intercept nested writes you need to wrap them in their own Proxies recursively.

q: You need to execute 10 API calls but limit concurrency to 3 at a time. What approach do you use?
options: Promise.all() with all 10 promises
Sequential await in a for loop
A concurrency-limited queue that fills slots as they free up
setTimeout to stagger the calls
explain: Promise.all() fires all 10 at once. Sequential await is too slow. A concurrency-limited queue processes a batch and only starts new calls as slots free up.

q: You use Object.freeze() on an object with a nested object. Can the nested object's properties be changed?
options: No freeze is recursive by default
Yes freeze is shallow — nested objects are not frozen
Only if the nested object was created after freeze was called
No but you will get a warning not an error
explain: Object.freeze() is shallow. It freezes top-level properties but nested objects remain mutable. For deep immutability you need to recursively freeze all nested objects.

q: What is the real difference between closure-based private variables and class private fields using #?
options: There is no difference — they are functionally identical
# fields are enforced by the engine, closures rely on scope rules
Module pattern is faster than class private fields
# fields can be accessed with reflection tools
explain: Closure privacy relies on scope. Class private fields using # are enforced at the language level — even reflection tools cannot access them.
